column2: Why does vitamin B12 deficiency impair nucleotide synthesis even when total folate is adequate?
column3: Methionine synthase needs B12 to pass the methyl group from methyl tetrahydrofolate to homocysteine and regenerate tetrahydrofolate; without it, folate is trapped in the methyl form.

column2: What pathway does cystathionine beta-synthase serve, and what does its severe deficiency cause?
column3: It combines homocysteine with serine using pyridoxal phosphate, starting transsulfuration toward cysteine; severe deficiency causes homocystinuria with thrombosis, lens dislocation, skeletal and neurological effects.

column2: Why is folate treatment alone hazardous in vitamin B12 deficiency?
column3: Folate can correct the blood abnormalities, but B12 deficiency also impairs methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, raising methylmalonate, so neurological injury can progress.

column2: How are the hepatic and erythroid forms of delta-aminolevulinate synthase regulated differently?

column2: Which haem-synthesis enzymes does lead inhibit, and what is central to diagnosing lead poisoning?
column3: Lead inhibits aminolevulinate dehydratase and ferrochelatase; basophilic stippling may occur, but no single smear feature is diagnostic, so blood lead measurement and exposure history are central.

column2: Why can drugs, fasting, alcohol and hormones precipitate acute attacks in porphyria?
column3: They induce hepatic haem demand, so early precursors such as aminolevulinate and porphobilinogen accumulate behind the partial enzyme defect and cause acute neurovisceral attacks.

column2: Why do later haem-pathway defects cause photosensitivity while purely acute hepatic forms usually do not?
column3: Accumulated later porphyrinogens oxidise to photosensitising porphyrins that cause light-dependent skin injury, whereas early precursors produce neurovisceral attacks instead.

column2: Why are newborns at risk of kernicterus, and how does phototherapy help?
column3: Increased production, immature conjugation and enterohepatic recycling raise unconjugated bilirubin, whose unbound form crosses the immature blood-brain barrier; phototherapy converts it to more excretable isomers.
